title: MLB teams face tough calls on signings, trades as current labour deal runs out
summary: Major League Baseball teams have tough calls to make this month, as they scramble to get the players they want on their rosters during an off-season that may be truncated amid contentious labour…

image.caption: Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred is seen speaking to members of the media in Milwaukee last month. The league's owners are pushing to establish a salary cap in their sport, against strong opposition from pro baseball players. (Ashley Landis/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: MLB

Major League Baseball teams have tough calls to make this month, as they scramble to get the players they want on their rosters during an off-season that may be truncated amid contentious labour negotiations.
Off-season could be shortened if lockout occurs, as owners push for salary cap

MLB's collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, at which point a lockout is widely expected. That's because team owners are pushing to change the economic system of their game to limit how much teams can spend on their payrolls. This has received strong opposition from the players.
The two sides appear dug in. They've each amassed large war chests and MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has admitted concern that a long work stoppage could be coming.
For now, the league's 30 teams have the rest of November to get their organizations set up for next season, while the existing agreement winds down.

Bruce Meyer, the interim executive director of the Major League Baseball Players Association, has described the owners' push for a salary cap as a 'nuclear bomb' that will make labour negotiations much more difficult. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)
While organizations will have done their homework on what the next labour agreement could bring, no one knows what the final deal will be until it is reached.

Observers with front office experience say that teams navigating this moment will have to weigh their need to get better against the risk that contracts signed today could carry unforeseen consequences tomorrow.
Dan Duquette, a former baseball executive with three MLB franchises, expects teams may have to temper their spending plans to some extent, given the uncertainty.
"I think teams are going to tighten their belts and take a look at what their critical investments are for next season," he said in an interview with CBC News.

Tim Purpura, left, reacts to being doused with champagne by Houston Astros infielder Adam Everett on Oct. 2, 2005, the day the club clinched a wild card spot on the last day of the regular season. The Astros went to the World Series that year, with Purpura as team's general manager. (Richard Carson/Reuters)
Fellow former MLB executive Tim Purpura says teams will nonetheless be on the lookout for ways to improve their rosters, whether or not a new labour agreement is on the horizon.

"You've got to strike while the iron's hot and get in there," said Purpura, whose career in baseball included serving as the general manager of the Houston Astros for several seasons, including in 2005, when the team went to the World Series.
Preparing for the unknown
While there's no guarantee the team owners will get a salary cap enacted, the league's teams will still weigh the implications of a potential cap coming forward.
Purpura says it's the norm that teams have to prepare for a variety of scenarios when the off-season arrives, including labour shortages.

"When we were in those situations, we were constantly doing financial models to see, 'OK, if they change this rule, this is going to affect us in this way,'" said Purpura, who was working in baseball during the 1994 season in which a strike — also over a proposed salary cap — wiped out the World Series.
The owners threw MLB teams a change-up of sorts this week, when they suggested that a cap could be delayed until 2028, backing down from an earlier call to have a cap in 2027.

Milwaukee Brewers catcher William Contreras, the MVP of the recent World Series, is seen celebrating with fans during the victory parade held for the Brewers on Oct. 30. Milwaukee won this year's World Series, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)

Under this revised proposal, teams would be obligated to limit spending to a hard cap of $258.2 million US — a level that would require eight high-spending MLB teams, including the Toronto Blue Jays, to trim payroll to meet such requirements for 2028.

The owners also want teams to achieve a minimum spend of $180.2 million US — and management says 12 MLB teams, including the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers, would have to boost their payroll to reach this threshold.
'A prudent way to go'
Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro has been through labour negotiations in the sport before, and says the plan is the same this time around — cap or no cap.
Blue Jays front office speaks after end of disappointing season
"You prepare under the current system and then you adjust along the way," he told media at the end of the season.
"That's a prudent way to go," said Duquette, who served as the general manager of the Montreal Expos in the early '90s.
But Duquette said it's hard for organizations to make long-term investments — such as player contracts — if they lack certainty in what the rules are going to be in a new labour deal.

He points to a moment from the '90s, when he was in talks with the Boston Red Sox about joining their organization (which he did, leaving the Expos to become the general manager of the Red Sox, ahead of the 1994 season).

Dan Duquette is seen speaking to then-Baltimore Orioles manager Buck Showalter during spring training in February 2014. Duquette was the Orioles' executive vice-president for baseball operations. (Gene J. Puskar/The Associated Press)
Boston had plans to build up its capacity to recruit international players, but Duquette said the organization waited to make that investment until the next labour agreement was a done deal.
"When they have certainty, they can go ahead and invest," said Duquette, who also held an executive role with the Baltimore Orioles.
The flip-side of this situation is that any contractual obligations that teams have already inked with players don't go away just because a new labour agreement comes into effect.
"The obligations that the teams have made to date, those remain club obligations," said Duquette.
Free agency begins
The off-season is the time that teams can use to improve their rosters for the year to come — whether via signing free agents, trading player contracts, or through other transactions.

Starting pitcher Tarik Skubal is seen delivering a pitch for the Los Angeles Dodgers, during Game 1 of the National League Championship Series in October. Skubal is a free agent this off-season and one of the marquee pitchers available to sign. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
Some observers believe the short window of time left on the current MLB labour agreement will spur the parties involved to get things done while there is certainty about the rules of engagement.

"There's a lot of pressure, in my opinion — on the GMs, on the agents, on the players — to get transactions done," Jim Bowden, a former general manager of the Cincinnati Reds and also the Washington Nationals, told the Foul Territory podcast.
MLB's free agency period got underway late on Monday. This is the time of year when teams can sign any players who lack contractual obligations to any clubs.
In the first few days of free agency, no major free agent signings had been announced. That's not unusual for the rhythm of baseball's free agent market, which tends to pick up later in the fall.
But any fears of a potential lockout did not appear to have ignited an immediate signing frenzy.
With files from The Associated Press
